title: A mercy to the worlds
hook: We sent you only as a mercy to all the worlds (21:107)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zakariyya in the sanctuary, and your line was don't leave me alone. Who did you message who might be lonely? Day four hundred eighty-four.

For most of this surah, the prophets have been passing by one at a time. Ibrahim in the fire. Lut. Nuh. Dawud and Sulayman. Ayyub, Yunus, Zakariyya, Maryam. Name after name, and the surah is named for them: Al-Anbiya, the Prophets. Then, near the end, the camera turns. It stops looking back at them and looks straight at the one hearing the surah first, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and sums up his whole mission in one line. Today, that line.

Verse one hundred seven. Pickthall: "We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples." In Arabic, rahmatan lil-'alamin. A mercy for the worlds. That last word, 'alamin, is the same one from the very first page of the Qur'an: praise belongs to God, Lord of the 'alamin, Lord of the Worlds. Pickthall translates it peoples here, and worlds there. Both are fair. Some commentators say it reaches past people: humans, jinn, animals, everything that is. And notice the shape of the sentence. Not save as: only as. The verse doesn't call mercy one part of his mission among others. It says he was sent only as mercy. There's a hadith in Muslim's collection. Once, he was asked to curse the idolaters who opposed him. He said he was not sent to curse; he was sent as a mercy. And the mercy keeps reaching past people. Bukhari records his story of a man, desperately thirsty himself, who climbed down into a well, filled his shoe with water and gave it to a dog panting at the edge, and God forgave him. The companions asked, is there reward even for animals? He said, in every living, breathing thing there is reward. So a mercy to the worlds isn't only a title. It sets a standard for anyone who follows him: the dog at the well counts. The ant counts. The stranger counts.
screen: `NOT SAVE AS A MERCY.` · `'ALAMIN: THE SAME WORD AS PAGE ONE.` · `NOT SENT TO CURSE.` · `WATER FOR A DOG AT THE WELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be a mercy to one creature. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then look around your day for one living thing you could ease. A plant on the windowsill that needs water. A bird that would take a dish of it. A pet that wants ten minutes of your attention. A person who's been short with you. Choose one, and picture doing it, slowly, in detail. If you pray, you can ask to be a little more like the one sent as a mercy. The bell holds the time.
A mercy to the worlds. Rahmatan lil-'alamin. The Prophet's whole mission in one line, reaching people, animals and everything that is. Today's word.
screen: `A MERCY TO THE WORLDS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a mercy to the worlds. Today, do the thing you pictured: one bowl of water, one plant, one patient answer. Day four hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims often quote 21:107 when describing the Prophet's character, and stories of his kindness to animals, like the man who gave water to a dog, are often taught to children.

fork.setup: you're desperately thirsty. you climb down a well and drink. back at the top, a dog is panting, licking the damp ground. what do you do?
options: walk on. you've had your water.
go back down, fill your shoe, and carry water up.
wave someone else over to help it.
fork.reveal: he climbed back down and carried water up in his shoe, and God forgave him for it. Bukhari records the story.

original.note: Arabic: a mercy to the worlds, 21:107.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice title for the Prophet.
what it means: the verse says his whole mission was sent only as mercy, and the mercy reaches every kind of creature.
what a scholar hears: the restrictive 'wa ma arsalnaka illa' (not save as); 'alamin echoes 1:2; commentators debate whether the mercy covers believers and unbelievers alike in this world.

sources.quoted: We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples.
